title: Retinal detachment
intro: The retina is the light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye. In retinal detachment it peels away from its supporting tissue, which can cause permanent vision loss if not treated promptly. It is painless but urgent. Sudden flashes, new floaters or a shadow across your vision need same-day assessment.

sections.heading: Causes and risk factors
paragraphs: Most detachments start with a tear or hole in the retina, often after the jelly-like vitreous inside the eye shrinks and pulls on it. Fluid then seeps behind the retina. Risk is higher with severe short-sightedness, previous cataract surgery, eye injury, earlier detachment in the other eye and family history.

sections.heading: Warning signs
paragraphs: Typical warning signs are sudden flashes of light, a sudden shower of new floaters, a dark curtain or shadow spreading across part of the visual field, or sudden blurred vision. The condition does not cause pain or redness. Any of these signs requires urgent examination by an eye doctor, ideally on the same day.

sections.heading: Diagnosis
paragraphs: An eye specialist dilates the pupil and examines the retina with a special lens and light to find tears and detachment. Ultrasound may be used if the view is blocked by bleeding. Tears detected early can often be treated before they detach.

sections.heading: Treatment
paragraphs: Small tears can be sealed with laser or freezing treatment in the clinic. Detached retinas need surgery. Options include vitrectomy, in which the vitreous is removed and a gas bubble or oil presses the retina back, and scleral buckling, in which a silicone band is fixed around the eye. After surgery with a gas bubble you may need to keep your head in a set position for days, and air travel or high altitude must be avoided until the gas has gone.
Most detachments can be repaired, though vision may not fully return, and sometimes more than one operation is needed.

sections.heading: After the operation
paragraphs: Use eye drops as prescribed, avoid heavy lifting and strenuous activity as advised and attend all follow-up visits. Report pain, redness or loss of vision at once, and report any new symptoms in the other eye right away.

examples.title: Acting fast
examples.text: Imagine you notice a dark shadow in the corner of your vision with flashing lights. You could go directly to an eye emergency service and ask someone to drive you.

examples.title: Positioning after surgery
examples.text: Suppose your surgeon asks you to lie face down for several days. You might arrange pillows, a face-down support and help at home ahead of time.
